subject: Chemistry
title: Plutonium: Made by Humans
description: A quick win: understand Plutonium: Made by Humans.

hook.text: Plutonium barely exists in nature. Almost every atom of it on Earth was created by humans in reactors.

buildup.text: Glenn Seaborg's team created it in 1940 by bombarding uranium with deuterons in a cyclotron.

discovery.text: They named it plutonium after Pluto, following uranium (Uranus) and neptunium (Neptune).

twist.text: Its existence was kept top secret during WWII. It powered the bomb dropped on Nagasaki in 1945.

climax.text: Plutonium also powers deep-space probes. Voyager 1 has been running on it since 1977.

punchline.text: Made by humans, named after Pluto. It powers bombs and Voyager.

quiz.question: Why does plutonium barely exist in nature?
options: It decays relatively quickly and must be made artificially in reactors

details.summary: Plutonium was first synthesized by Glenn Seaborg's team at Berkeley in 1940 by bombarding uranium-238 with deuterons. Named after the planet Pluto following the naming convention of uranium and neptunium, plutonium-239 turned out to be fissile.
details.whyItMatters: Plutonium demonstrated that human-made elements could have world-changing consequences. It powers nuclear weapons and spacecraft while posing severe nuclear proliferation and waste challenges.
takeaways: Plutonium was synthesized at Berkeley in 1940 following uranium and neptunium
Plutonium-239 undergoes nuclear fission, releasing enormous energy
It was used in the Fat Man bomb and continues to power deep-space missions

faq.question: Why was plutonium's discovery kept secret during World War II?
faq.answer: Plutonium's fissile properties made it a potential nuclear weapon material. Its discovery was classified under the Manhattan Project immediately. Seaborg's team could not publish their findings until after the atomic bombings of Japan in 1945..

faq.question: How does plutonium power spacecraft so far from the Sun?
faq.answer: Plutonium-238 generates heat through radioactive decay without needing sunlight. Radioisotope thermoelectric generators convert this heat to electricity using thermoelectric materials..
